front.title: Probabilistic Contact Metadata for DTN Bundle Routing

abstract.t: This document defines a generic uncertainty propagation layer for Delay/Disruption Tolerant Networking (DTN) routing: the Contact Probability Block (CPB), a BPv7 extension block that carries probability metadata in-bundle between forwarding nodes. The contribution is the standardized transport mechanism rather than any single routing algorithm; CPB is designed to be consumed and produced by heterogeneous DTN routing protocols (PRoPHET, CGR, MaxProp, RAPID, Spray-and-Wait) without requiring changes to those algorithms themselves.

The specification uses CBOR floating-point encoding in bundle extension blocks, with half-precision (IEEE 754 binary16) recommended for bandwidth efficiency. The extension preserves endpoint identifier immutability, is backwards-compatible with BPv7, and integrates with existing security mechanisms (BPSec). Distinct probability semantics from different routing families are kept separable via an explicit metric-type tag; cross-metric arithmetic is prohibited.

This document is Experimental. The accompanying simulation study validates that experimental routing policies consuming per-contact confidence metadata from CPB blocks can materially outperform confidence-blind baseline CGR under adversarial conditions with rate-aware costing. The contribution of this specification is the standardized BPv7 extension block for carrying that metadata. Operational deployment questions — robustness to noisy/adversarial estimates, control-theoretic stability under feedback, and real interoperability with production BP stacks — are explicitly enumerated as open issues and not claimed as resolved by this document.

section.name: Introduction
section.t: Delay-tolerant networks (DTNs) often face uncertain contact schedules, such as during Mars mission disruptions, where standard BPv7 routing like Contact Graph Routing (CGR) may delay delivery due to reliance on fixed contact plans. Probabilistic routing metadata enables adaptive forwarding decisions by communicating contact likelihood estimates between nodes.

This specification defines a bundle extension block (the Contact Probability Block, or CPB) for carrying probabilistic contact metadata, enabling efficient routing decisions in DTNs for applications like space exploration communications.

section.name: Problem Statement (IPNSIG SSI Architecture, Section 4.2)
section.t: The Interplanetary Networking Special Interest Group (IPNSIG), the Interplanetary Chapter of the Internet Society, published "Solar System Internet Architecture and Governance — from the Moon to Mars and beyond" in September 2023 . Section 4.2 ("Routing and Forwarding") of that document frames the routing problem this specification addresses:

blockquote.t: The routing and forwarding procedures of the terrestrial Internet would not adapt well in the Solar System Internet, as topological state information could not be provided in a timely manner due to the lengthy signal propagation delays, frequent lapses of connectivity, and dynamic topology... New technology is needed.

section.t: The first "Considerations" bullet of IPNSIG Section 4.2 directly invites the design approach taken by this specification:

blockquote.t: By what delay-tolerant mechanism(s) does this technology obtain the information on which it decides which next-hop node to forward a given bundle to? Does it do so by route computation, by scoring and/or preferential ranking of neighboring nodes, or in some other way?

section.t: The Contact Probability Block defined here is precisely such a "scoring and/or preferential ranking" signal, carried in-bundle as metadata for forwarding nodes to consult. The CPB design responds directly to two of IPNSIG Section 4.2's four numbered Recommendations:

dl.dd: "routing and forwarding technologies are needed that do not require continuous human intervention or management from Earth." CPB enables autonomous, in-bundle probability annotation that each forwarder consults locally, without round-trips to Earth.

"Autonomy, in turn, requires standard methods of: propagating whatever information is needed to support route computation; utilizing that information in common ways that assure coherent forwarding." CPB standardizes both the wire format for propagating probability information () and the precedence and matching rules for utilizing it (, ).

section.t: positions CPB relative to the routing-protocol families catalogued in IPNSIG Section 4.2 and its Appendix A: PRoPHET , Spray and Wait , Schedule-Aware Bundle Routing (SABR), Contact Graph Routing (CGR), and Opportunistic CGR with Uncertain Contact Plans (CGR-UCoP) . CPB is a cross-protocol metadata layer, not a replacement for any of these algorithms; each can consume or produce CPB data.

section.name: Motivation
section.t: Standard DTN routing protocols operate with deterministic contact schedules or historical encounter statistics. However, in highly disrupted networks:

ul.li: Contact schedules change unpredictably (dust storms on Mars, solar weather, orbital variations)
Historical data becomes stale
Coordinated path computation elements (PCEs) can estimate probabilities but need a way to communicate them to forwarding nodes
Adaptive routing decisions require explicit probability metadata at the bundle level

section.t: By embedding probability estimates directly in bundles as a standard extension block, this specification enables all DTN routing protocols to benefit from more informed forwarding decisions.

section.name: Requirements Language
section.t: The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 when, and only when, they appear in all capitals, as shown here.

dl.dd: The likelihood of successful bundle delivery to a destination node via a particular next hop or path, expressed as a value in [0.0, 1.0].
A bundle extension block that carries contact probability metadata, routing hints, and temporal context.
A probability estimate specific to a particular next-hop neighbor or outgoing interface.
An overall or baseline probability estimate when per-path probabilities are unavailable.
An identifier distinguishing the semantic meaning of the probability value (e.g., PRoPHET delivery predictability, CGR contact confidence, MaxProp path reliability).
The time period (in seconds) after creation during which the probability estimate remains usable for routing decisions.

section.name: Notation Conventions
section.t: This document uses three distinct notations for describing data structures, following the conventions of other DTN Working Group drafts:

dl.dd: Formal schema definitions per . Listings are labeled "type: cddl". CDDL defines the structural constraints that implementations MUST conform to.
Human-readable representations of CBOR data per Appendix G. Listings are labeled "type: cbor-diag". EDN examples show concrete data values in readable form.
Base-16 encoded wire format with inline comments. Listings are labeled "type: hex". These show the exact byte sequences that appear on the wire.

section.name: Architectural Considerations
section.t: This section explains the architectural rationale for using bundle extension blocks rather than URI query parameters for probabilistic routing metadata.

section.name: Why NOT URI Query Parameters
section.t: An earlier design considered encoding probability as a URI query parameter in the destination EID:
This approach violates fundamental DTN principles for the following reasons:

section.name: Endpoint Identifier Immutability
section.t: Endpoint identifiers (EIDs) are immutable addresses that uniquely identify bundle destinations. If routing metadata were embedded in EIDs:

ul.li: Intermediate routers would need to modify destination addresses to update or strip probability parameters
This violates the end-to-end principle and the Bundle Protocol specification
Routers cannot determine whether ipn:100.1?prob=0.75 and ipn:100.1?prob=0.5 represent the same or different endpoints
Destination nodes would receive bundles with varying EID formats depending on router processing
EID-based duplicate detection would fail when the same logical endpoint has multiple representations
Custody transfer mechanisms would malfunction

section.name: Router Modification Problem
section.t: If probability were in the destination EID, the following scenario occurs:

ol.li: Router A receives a bundle destined to ipn:100.1?prob=0.75
Router A consults the probability for forwarding decisions

ul.li: Forward as-is with ?prob=0.75 (but this value may be stale/incorrect for the next hop)
Strip the parameter to ipn:100.1 (modifying the destination address)
Update the parameter to a new value, e.g., ?prob=0.6 (also modifying the destination address)

ol.li: Any modification violates the immutability principle and breaks downstream systems

section.t: This architectural violation is unacceptable in the DTN model.

section.name: Solution: Bundle Extension Blocks
section.t: This specification resolves the architectural conflict by carrying probabilistic metadata in bundle extension blocks, completely separate from endpoint identifiers:

ul.li: Destination EID remains immutable and unchanged: ipn:100.1
Routing metadata travels in extension blocks (the Contact Probability Block)
Routers can freely add, remove, or modify metadata without affecting the destination EID
Security is maintained independently using Bundle Integrity Blocks (BIBs)
Legacy nodes safely ignore unknown extension blocks without affecting bundle delivery

section.t: This design maintains clean architectural separation between:

ul.li: Addressing (EIDs): immutable, end-to-end
Routing Hints (CPB metadata): mutable, hop-by-hop

section.name: Overview
section.t: The Contact Probability Block (CPB) is a standard BPv7 bundle extension block that carries contact probability metadata. Its purpose is to communicate probability estimates from source nodes, path computation elements (PCEs), or intermediate routers to downstream forwarding nodes.

section.name: Block Structure
section.t: The CPB has the standard bundle extension block structure defined in . The canonical block structure is a CBOR array per RFC 9171 Section 4.3.2:

The block-type-specific data (BTSD) field is a CBOR byte string (bstr) whose content is a CBOR-encoded cpb-data map. This byte-string embedding follows RFC 9171's canonical block structure, where the BTSD type is bstr (not any). The formal CDDL binding follows below.
The following annotated hex shows a concrete CPB with prob=0.75 for destination node 100:

figure.name: CPB Concrete Example (type: hex)
figure.sourcecode: 18 C8 ; type=200 (exp per RFC9171 §9.1) 02 ; num=2 11 ; flags=0x11 (replicate; drop if bad) 00 ; crc=0 (none) 57 ; BTSD: bstr (23 bytes) A4 ; map with 4 entries 00 F93A00 ; 0: prob=0.75 (float16) 01 81 ; 1: array of 1 path entry 82 ; [node, prob] 18 64 ; node=100 F93C00 ; prob=1.0 02 1A 00F73A80 ; 2: timestamp (DTN epoch) 04 19 0E10 ; 4: validity=3600s F6 ; crc: null

section.t: The CBOR data structure in the block-data field is defined as follows. The BTSD is byte-string-embedded per RFC 9171's canonical block structure, using the CDDL socket and generic rules from RFC 9171 Section 4.3.2:

figure.name: CPB Extension Block Binding (type: cddl)
figure.sourcecode:
; Integration with RFC 9171 canonical block structure. ; The BTSD is a bstr whose content is CBOR-encoded cpb-data. ; The "/ bstr" alternative permits encrypted BTSD (BCB-wrapped ; content from a security context that encrypts the BTSD before ; the CPB's own processing; see Section 7.2.3 for CPB-specific ; BCB prohibition on the CPB itself).
$extension-block /= extension-block-use<200, (bstr .cbor cpb-data / bstr)>

figure.name: CPB Data Structure (type: cddl)
figure.sourcecode:
cpb-data = { ? 0: probability, ; Default/overall probability ? 1: [* path-entry], ; Per-path probabilities ? 2: uint, ; Timestamp (DTN epoch seconds) ? 3: bstr, ; Source PCE identifier (optional) ? 4: uint, ; Validity duration (seconds, TTL) ? 5: metric-type, ; Metric type identifier ? 6: probability, ; Confidence/variance estimate * (int .gt 6) => any ; Extensibility (future fields) }
probability = float ; See Section 3.4 for encoding
path-entry = [ next-hop: eid-reference, ; Next-hop node identifier probability: float ; Probability for this path ]
eid-reference = uint / bstr ; Node number or full EID
metric-type = &( prophet-dp: 0, ; PRoPHET delivery predictability cgr-confidence: 1, ; CGR contact confidence maxprop-cost: 2, ; MaxProp path cost (inverted) rapid-utility: 3, ; RAPID utility metric generic: 4, ; Unspecified/generic probability ) / uint ; Extensible via future assignment

section.t: Note on bstr .cbor embedding: The CDDL .cbor control operator ( Section 3.8.4) indicates that the byte string contains valid CBOR matching the cpb-data rule. The plain bstr alternative accommodates cases where the BTSD has been encrypted by a security context applied to the enclosing extension block structure; in this case the original CBOR content is opaque until decryption.

dl.dd: An overall probability estimate when per-path data is unavailable. Range [0.0, 1.0].
An array of [next-hop, probability] tuples. Implementations MUST limit to a maximum of 8 entries ().
Creation time in DTN epoch seconds (seconds since 2000-01-01 00:00:00 UTC, per Section 4.3.1). Enables receivers to compute age and apply probability decay.
An opaque byte string identifying the entity that computed the probability. Used for trust evaluation.

The number of seconds after the timestamp during which this probability estimate remains usable. When the sum of timestamp and validity duration is less than the current time, the CPB is expired and SHOULD be treated as if the default probability (field 0) were absent. If omitted, implementations SHOULD apply deployment-specific age thresholds ().
Identifies the semantic meaning of the probability value. When absent, implementations SHOULD treat the value as generic (type 4).

An optional float value in [0.0, 1.0] representing the confidence or certainty in the probability estimate. A confidence of 0.9 with P = 0.5 (based on 1000 observations) carries more weight than confidence of 0.1 with P = 0.5 (based on 2 observations). Routing algorithms MAY use this for risk-aware forwarding.

section.name: Block Processing Flags
section.t: The CPB MUST set the block processing control flags ( Section 4.4.1) as follows:

ul.li: Bit 0 (0x01): Replicate in all fragments: Implementers MUST set this bit so that if a bundle with a CPB is fragmented during transmission, each fragment carries a copy of the CPB.
Bit 4 (0x10): Discard if can't process: Implementers MUST set this bit because the CPB is advisory routing metadata, not critical to bundle delivery.
Bits 1-3, 5-7: Leave as 0 (reserved).

section.t: In practice, both flags set means the block processing flags byte is set to 0x11 (binary 00010001).

Path-entry handling under fragmentation: When replicating a CPB into a fragment, the fragmenting node MAY prune path-entry elements (field 1) that are known to be unreachable in the fragment's remaining path, but MUST NOT alter the probability values of retained entries. The default-probability field (0) and metric-type field (5) MUST NOT be modified during fragmentation.

section.name: Cyclic Redundancy Check (CRC) Handling
section.t: The block-data CRC field ( Section 4.4.1) is optional:

ul.li: No CRC (recommended): Set crc-type to 0 and crc field to CBOR null (0xF6). This is the default and minimizes overhead.
Optional CRC: Implementations MAY include CRC type 1 (16-bit Fletcher) or type 2 (32-bit CRC).

section.t: Implementations SHOULD prefer BPSec BIBs () over CRCs for integrity, as BIBs provide both authentication and integrity.

section.name: Hop Count Block Co-Presence
section.t: Bundles carrying a CPB SHOULD also carry a Hop Count block (block type 10, Section 4.4.2). The Hop Count block provides a loop termination guarantee independent of probability-based routing decisions.

section.name: Block Type Code
section.t: The bundle extension block format () requires each extension block to have a type code that identifies what kind of block it is.

section.name: IANA Registration

ul.li: Implementations MAY use values in the 192-254 range for experimental/private use
The example hex dump uses code 200 (0xC8) for illustration
Production deployments SHOULD use the IANA-assigned code

section.name: Backwards Compatibility
section.t: Routers that don't recognize the CPB block type code will:

ol.li: Check the block processing control flags (byte 2 in the extension block)
If flags indicate "discard if can't process", drop the block silently
If flags indicate "remove if can't process", strip it before forwarding
Continue routing the bundle using remaining blocks (backwards compatible)

section.name: CBOR Encoding of Probability Values
section.t: The CDDL schema () defines probability fields as float rather than constraining to a specific precision, because enforcing float16 in CDDL is difficult for encoders to implement in practice. Instead, the precision requirement is expressed as a prose recommendation:

Implementations SHOULD choose probability values that are exactly representable in IEEE 754 binary16 (half-precision). All values in [0.0, 1.0] at routing-grade precision (~0.001 granularity from the 10-bit mantissa) are representable in binary16. When a value is representable in float16, Section 4.2.1's deterministic encoding requirement ensures it will be encoded in 3 bytes.

ul.li: Range: [0.0, 1.0], sufficient for all probability values
Precision: Approximately 3 decimal digits, adequate for routing decisions
Overhead: 3 bytes per value when float16 is used
Standard: Defined in (CBOR specification)

section.t: Implementations that produce probability values not representable in float16 will incur 5 bytes (float32) or 9 bytes (float64) per value under deterministic encoding. Receivers MUST accept any valid CBOR float encoding and clamp the decoded value to [0.0, 1.0].

Bandwidth Considerations and Array Limits: A CPB with per-path probabilities to multiple relays adds overhead (~4-5 bytes per entry). To prevent DoS via oversized arrays on low-bandwidth links, implementations MUST limit the per-path array (field 1) to a maximum of 8 entries. CPBs with more than 8 path-entry elements MUST be treated as malformed and discarded, with the event logged per Section 4.3 for DTNMA correlation. This limit is normative; both encoders and decoders MUST enforce it.

section.name: Invalid Float Handling
section.t: Implementations MUST handle invalid or out-of-range probability values as follows:

ul.li: NaN (0xF97E00): MUST be rejected as malformed.
+/-Infinity (0xF97C00, 0xF9FC00): MUST be rejected as malformed.
Negative values: Treat as 0.0 (invalid probability).
Values > 1.0: Treat as 1.0 (certainty).
Subnormal values: SHOULD be flushed to zero for embedded FPU compatibility.
Malformed CBOR: Discard the CPB block and continue processing the bundle.

section.t: In all error cases, implementations SHOULD log the error (including source, timestamp, and offending value) for debugging. Malformed CBOR MUST never cause bundle deletion or administrative action; the CPB is advisory and bundle processing continues regardless.

section.name: Encoding Details
section.t: When a probability value is representable in half-precision, the CBOR encoding uses major type 7 with additional information value 25 (16-bit IEEE 754 binary16):

figure.name: CBOR Encoding: Major Type 7, Additional Info 25
figure.artwork: Major Type: 7 (floating-point or simple) Additional Info: 25 (16-bit IEEE 754 float) Total Bytes: 3 (tag byte 0xF9 + 2 float bytes)

table.name: CBOR Encodings for Common Probability Values

section.name: Metric-Type Semantics and Cross-Metric Comparison
section.t: The probability values carried in a CPB are dimensionless numbers in [0.0, 1.0], but their semantics differ substantially across routing protocols. The metric-type field (field 5, ) distinguishes these semantics. This subsection specifies the constraints on combining values across metric types.
The defined metric types carry the following distinct semantics:

dl.dd: PRoPHET delivery predictability, an empirical encounter-history statistic computed locally by each node per . Reflects observed past behavior, not a forward-looking estimate.

Per-contact success probability against a known contact schedule. Reflects forward-looking confidence in a planned contact occurring as scheduled (link availability, atmospheric conditions, antenna pointing).
Inverted path cost from MaxProp. Lower MaxProp cost is mapped to higher CPB probability. The inversion is lossy; the original cost magnitude is not recoverable from the CPB value.
Per-packet utility function value from RAPID. Reflects an optimization-derived score, not a direct probability of delivery.
Unspecified semantic. The producer makes no claim beyond "value in [0.0, 1.0]". Consumers SHOULD NOT assume any specific interpretation.

section.t: Cross-metric arithmetic is prohibited. A router MUST NOT combine values from different metric types via arithmetic (addition, multiplication, weighted averaging, etc.) and treat the result as a meaningful probability. A PRoPHET predictability of 0.7 and a CGR confidence of 0.7 are not interchangeable inputs to the same routing decision. Specifically:

ul.li: A router implementing a rate-aware confidence-weighted policy that consumes CPB data (for example, a policy whose cost function resembles formulations in prior work such as CGR-UCoP ) MUST use only metric-type 1 (cgr-confidence) values, and MUST treat path-entries of other metric types as if absent.
A router applying PRoPHET-style transitivity rules MUST use only metric-type 0 (prophet-dp) values, and similarly ignore others.
A router consuming metric-type 4 (generic) SHOULD treat the value as advisory only and MUST NOT use it as the sole input to a routing decision.

section.t: Mixed-metric CPBs: A single CPB instance carries one metric-type (field 5). A bundle MAY carry multiple CPBs with different metric types simultaneously (for example, a CPB with cgr-confidence from a PCE and a separate CPB with prophet-dp accumulated at intermediate hops). The precedence rules of apply within a metric type; across metric types, each CPB is consumed only by routers implementing that metric's algorithm. A router that does not understand a particular metric type MUST ignore that CPB and continue processing.

Metric-type registry policy: Future routing protocols defining new probability semantics SHOULD register a new metric-type code (see ) rather than overloading an existing one. The CPB Metric Types sub-registry exists precisely to keep semantically distinct values separable on the wire.

Calibration and normalization: This document does not specify normalization between metric types because cross-metric equivalence has no rigorous theoretical foundation in the published DTN literature. Implementations that wish to combine evidence from multiple metrics for ranking purposes SHOULD do so using a documented, deployment-specific policy and SHOULD NOT rely on numerical comparability across types. This area is identified as an open research question in .

section.name: Multiple CPBs in One Bundle
section.t: A bundle may accumulate multiple Contact Probability Blocks as it traverses the network. When a bundle contains multiple CPBs with conflicting probabilities for the same destination, implementations SHOULD use the following precedence:

ol.li: Most recent timestamp (highest value)
If timestamps equal, trust the source (implementation-defined trust policy)
If timestamps are equal AND sources are equally trusted, prefer the CPB with the more specific metric-type (e.g., cgr-confidence over generic) for the current routing protocol
Default behavior: use the last encountered CPB (highest bundle block number)

section.t: Implementations MUST NOT fail or misroute when encountering multiple CPBs.

figure.name: CPB with Per-Path Probabilities (type: cbor-diag)
CPB Per-Path Wire Encoding (type: hex)
figure.artwork: A3 ; map with 3 entries 00 F93A00 ; key 0: default prob = 0.75 01 82 ; key 1: array with 2 path entries 82 ; path entry [node, prob] 19 012C F93800 ; node 300, prob 0.5 18 64 F93C00 ; node 100, prob 1.0 05 01 ; key 5: metric-type = cgr-confidence

section.name: Per-Path Matching Rules
section.t: When a router consults the per-path array:

ol.li: Match the next-hop node/EID against path-entry keys
If exact match found, use that probability
If no match found, use default probability (field 0)
If no default probability defined, use 0.5 (neutral)

section.t: EID-references in the path-entry array MUST match the destination bundle's URI scheme. For IPN bundles, node numbers are encoded as CBOR unsigned integers (per 's updated ipn URI scheme); for other schemes, encode the full EID as CBOR text string.

Scheme Mismatch Handling: When the next-hop scheme does not match the CPB's path-entry scheme, implementations fall back to the default probability (field 0); if no default is defined, use 0.5. Implementations SHOULD log the scheme mismatch for OAM correlation per Section 4.3.

section.name: Creation
section.t: The Contact Probability Block is created by:

ul.li: The source application (using historical or predicted contact data)
A path computation element (PCE) (using network-wide routing state)
The first-hop router (using local contact statistics)

section.t: Implementations SHOULD include a timestamp (field 2) and a validity duration (field 4). Timestamps MUST be expressed in seconds since 2000-01-01 00:00:00 UTC (DTN epoch, per Section 4.3.1).
In networks with significant propagation delays, clock synchronization is challenging. When validating a CPB timestamp, implementations SHOULD apply tolerance for clock drift and light-time delays:

ul.li: Forward skew tolerance: Apply a configurable drift threshold (default: +/-600 seconds). CPBs with timestamps > current time + drift threshold MUST be discarded.
Backward skew/age threshold: CPBs with timestamps < current time - max_age MUST be discarded (default max_age: 86400s interplanetary, 3600s terrestrial).
Deployment-specific adjustment: Networks SHOULD define explicit max_drift and max_age per link characteristics.

section.name: Processing by Intermediate Routers
section.t: When a router processes a bundle containing a CPB:

ol.li: Read: Consult the CPB's default or per-path probability values.
Decide: Use the probability as an input to routing decisions.
Update (optional): If the router has fresher probability data, it SHOULD append a new CPB block to the bundle (preserves any end-to-end integrity signatures protecting the original block).
Forward: Transmit the bundle with the CPB(s) to the next hop.

section.name: Usage in Routing Algorithms
section.t: Routing algorithms MAY use the CPB in several ways:

ul.li: Threshold-based: Forward if prob > threshold
Weighted selection: Choose proportionally to probability
Replication: Replicate to ceil(1/prob) contacts (epidemic/spray)
Priority: Prioritize higher-probability bundles during congestion
Risk-aware: Weight decisions by both probability and confidence (field 6)

section.name: Stability Considerations and Feedback Dynamics
section.t: Probability-aware forwarding creates feedback between routing decisions and observed network behavior. Naive use of CPB data can produce instability that confidence-blind routing avoids. Three dynamics are particularly relevant:

dl.dd: When multiple sources receive identical high-confidence CPB advertisements for the same relay, they all forward to that relay simultaneously. The relay congests, its actual delivery probability drops, but in-flight CPBs continue advertising the stale high confidence. Traffic remains herded until updated CPBs propagate, which in DTN timeframes can take hours.

If a router switches preferences whenever CPB values cross a threshold, small probability fluctuations near the threshold cause traffic to oscillate between routes. Each switch may itself generate new CPB observations that further perturb the values.

In dense topologies, simultaneous reaction by many routers to the same CPB update can produce correlated congestion events. This is structurally similar to TCP synchronization in IP networks but with much longer recovery cycles due to DTN propagation delays.

section.t: Implementations SHOULD mitigate these dynamics. The following techniques are RECOMMENDED:

ul.li: Hysteresis: Use distinct enter and exit thresholds (e.g., switch to a route at p > 0.75, switch away only at p < 0.60). Avoids threshold-crossing chatter on small fluctuations.
Rate limiting: Cap the frequency of routing preference changes per (source, destination) pair (e.g., at most one switch per contact opportunity, not per bundle).

Randomized tie-breaking: When multiple routes have CPB probabilities within a configurable epsilon (default: 0.05), select randomly rather than deterministically by lowest EID. Breaks herding without sacrificing the high-probability choice.

Probability decay under load: Maintain a local estimate of congestion on each next-hop and apply a load-aware discount to the received CPB probability before using it in routing decisions. Closes the feedback loop locally rather than waiting for upstream CPB refresh.
Bounded credulity: Cap how heavily any single CPB can influence the local routing decision relative to the router's own observations. Specific weights are deployment-dependent.

section.t: A formal control-theoretic stability analysis of CPB-driven feedback dynamics is not provided in this document; this is identified as an open research question in . Implementations that omit all of the above mitigations SHOULD NOT be deployed in production DTNs where congestion or herding could degrade service.

section.name: Relationship to Existing DTN Routing Protocols
section.t: This section positions CPB relative to the existing DTN routing-protocol families catalogued in IPNSIG Section 4.2 and its Appendix A ("Routing and Forwarding State of the Art").

section.name: PRoPHET (RFC 6693)
section.t: PRoPHET computes delivery predictability metrics at each node based on encounter history. A PRoPHET router can consume CPB data as additional input to its predictability calculations, or produce CPB entries with metric-type 0 (prophet-dp) based on its computed predictions.

section.name: MaxProp
section.t: MaxProp's drop policy (drop-least-expected-path-reliability) naturally benefits from explicit CPB probabilities (metric-type 2).

section.name: RAPID
section.t: RAPID's per-packet utility function can directly incorporate CPB probabilities (metric-type 3) instead of inferring delivery likelihood from history.

section.name: Spray-and-Wait Family
section.t: Spray-and-Wait limits replication to N copies sprayed to selected relays. Traditional Spray-and-Wait sprays uniformly at random; CPB enables probability-aware target selection.

section.name: Contact Graph Routing (CGR)
section.t: Contact Graph Routing computes optimal routes based on a deterministic contact schedule. CPB adds uncertainty metrics (metric-type 1, cgr-confidence). Extensions like CGR-UCoP (Contact Graph Routing with Uncertain Contact Plans, ) already incorporate contact failure probabilities; CPB provides a standardized wire format for this data. The closest architectural precedent is the CGR Extension Block , which demonstrated that in-band routing metadata in extension blocks was architecturally sound. reports an experiment in which several simulator-internal routing policies consume CPB-supplied confidences under adversarial conditions with rate-aware costing. CGR-UCoP is treated strictly as prior art for simulation validation, not the conceptual basis for CPB.

section.name: DTNMA (RFC 9675)
section.t: defines a DTN management architecture orthogonal to routing. A DTNMA agent could monitor CPB-related metrics (frequency of stale CPBs, scheme mismatches, BIB verification failures) for network health assessment.

section.name: Summary: CPB as Cross-Cutting Metadata
section.t: The Contact Probability Block is designed as a cross-protocol metadata layer rather than a replacement for existing algorithms. Each algorithm can optionally consume CPB data from upstream nodes or produce CPB data for downstream nodes, without requiring any internal changes to the algorithm itself.

ul.li: Nodes that do not recognize the CPB block type MUST ignore it and continue processing the bundle normally
The bundle's destination, source, and other standard fields are unaffected by the CPB
Legacy routing protocols (CGR, PRoPHET, MaxProp, RAPID, Spray-and-Wait) continue to function without the CPB
The CPB is optional; bundles without it use standard routing behavior
Untrusted networks: An attacker could inject false probability values to cause mis-routing (sinkhole via inflated, blackhole via deflated probabilities)
Stale data: A captured bundle with outdated probabilities could cause poor routing decisions
Inference attacks: Observing probability values over time could reveal traffic patterns or network topology

Route poisoning by semi-trusted relays: A relay that holds valid credentials within an administrative domain may still produce CPB advertisements that systematically bias routing decisions toward itself, away from a competitor, or against specific destinations
Replay of stale CPBs: An attacker captures a recent valid (BIB-signed) CPB and replays it later when the underlying conditions have changed

Inter-domain trust escalation: A CPB created by an entity trusted in one administrative domain crosses into a second domain where the producer is unknown; the second domain has no basis for trust evaluation

section.name: Trust Model
section.t: This document does not mandate a single trust model because DTN deployments span a wide range of administrative scenarios — from a single-operator interplanetary relay network to multi-party terrestrial mesh deployments. Instead, this subsection identifies the trust questions every CPB deployment MUST answer in its local trust policy, and provides default guidance.

section.name: Who is Authorized to Append CPBs
section.t: By default, any node along the bundle's path MAY append a CPB. This is permissive and suitable for low-stakes deployments where the cost of bad routing is recoverable. For higher-stakes deployments, the local trust policy SHOULD restrict CPB authorship to a named set of authorized PCEs (identified by the source PCE identifier field, field 3), or to nodes possessing a specific BPSec credential. CPBs from unauthorized sources SHOULD be discarded, with the event logged per Section 4.3.

section.name: Cryptographic Adjudication of Conflicting CPBs
section.t: When a bundle carries multiple CPBs from different sources with conflicting probabilities, the precedence rules of select one. Those rules SHOULD be evaluated only after BIB verification of each CPB; unsigned or BIB-invalid CPBs MUST be excluded from the precedence calculation in trust-policy contexts that require authentication. A receiver MUST NOT apply the metric-type-specificity tie-breaker ( step 3) to elevate a less-trusted source over a more-trusted one; trust ranking takes precedence over metric specificity.

section.name: Downstream Handling of Upstream BIBs
section.t: A downstream router that cannot verify an upstream BIB (missing key material, expired credentials, unrecognized security context) has two acceptable behaviors:

ul.li: Strict: Treat the unverifiable CPB as absent for routing decisions, and forward the bundle unchanged so that downstream routers with the correct credentials may still consume it. This is RECOMMENDED as the default.

Permissive: Use the unverified CPB advisorily, treating it as metric-type 4 (generic) regardless of its declared metric-type. This is NOT RECOMMENDED in adversarial environments but may be appropriate in cooperative single-operator deployments where credential rollout lags CPB adoption.

section.t: A router MUST NOT silently strip an unverifiable BIB-protected CPB and re-sign it with its own credentials; doing so launders provenance and breaks the append-only trust chain. If a router needs to express a different probability estimate, it MUST append a new CPB with its own BIB rather than modifying or replacing the original.

section.name: Route Poisoning by Semi-Trusted Relays
section.t: A relay that is trusted enough to participate in the network but not trusted to make routing decisions for the entire domain can still degrade routing by producing biased CPB advertisements. Defenses against this attack model are imperfect at the CPB layer; mitigations SHOULD include:

ul.li: Plausibility checks: a receiver SHOULD compare the asserted CPB probability against locally observed delivery statistics for the same next-hop, and discount or discard CPBs that deviate beyond a deployment-specific tolerance (default: factor of 2).

Source reputation: trust policies MAY maintain per-source reputation scores derived from historical accuracy, and weight CPBs by source reputation when consuming them. CPB itself does not specify a reputation mechanism; the DTN Management Architecture () is the appropriate vehicle.
Bounded influence (): cap how much any single CPB can shift the local routing decision relative to the router's own observations.

section.t: None of these mitigations defeat a sufficiently capable adversary; they raise the cost of route poisoning to make casual misbehavior detectable. Trust frameworks that close this gap (e.g., formal reputation aggregation, attestation chains) are out of scope for this document.

section.name: Inter-Domain Trust
section.t: When a bundle carrying a CPB crosses an administrative boundary, the receiving domain has no a priori basis for trusting the CPB's producer. Inter-domain trust SHOULD be established via one of:

ul.li: A bilateral or multilateral trust agreement that designates which PCE identifiers and BIB credentials from the foreign domain are accepted

A gateway router at the domain boundary that consumes the foreign CPB advisorily, validates it against local observations, and (optionally) appends a domain-native CPB expressing the gateway's translated assessment
A policy of discarding all CPBs at the domain boundary, with the receiving domain regenerating CPBs internally from its own observations

section.t: This document does not standardize inter-domain trust establishment; deployments SHOULD document their inter-domain CPB policy explicitly. This area is identified as an open question in .

section.name: Replay Resistance
section.t: The timestamp field (field 2) and validity duration field (field 4), combined with the forward and backward skew tolerances of , provide replay resistance proportional to the configured age threshold. Strong replay resistance requires additionally that BIB protection covers the timestamp; an attacker that can edit the timestamp without invalidating the BIB defeats this mechanism. Implementations MUST ensure the BIB security target list includes the entire CPB block, not just a subset of its fields.

section.name: Integrity Protection
section.t: For deployments in untrusted networks or where source authentication is required, the CPB MUST be protected using Bundle Integrity Blocks (BIBs) as defined in (BPSec).

section.name: Source CPB with Append-Only Intermediates
section.t: The source creates a CPB and attaches a BIB protecting only that CPB's block number. Intermediate routers with fresher probability estimates append new CPB blocks without modifying the source's CPB.

section.name: Strip-and-Replace Model
section.t: As an alternative, implementations MAY use a strip-and-replace model where each forwarder validates the previous CPB, removes it, inserts a fresh CPB with its own probability estimate, and signs it with its own BIB. Deployments SHOULD choose one model per administrative domain and document the policy.

section.name: Prohibition on BCB Encryption
section.t: Implementations MUST NOT encrypt the CPB using a Block Confidentiality Block (BCB). Encrypting a routing-critical extension block renders it opaque to the forwarding nodes that need it. Integrity protection (BIB) is appropriate; confidentiality protection (BCB) is not.

ul.li: Signature verification before using CPB for critical routing decisions
Timestamp validation (discard old or future-dated CPBs)
Secondary validation against local contact statistics
Conservative thresholds for critical payloads

section.name: Privacy Considerations
section.t: CPB metadata may reveal information about network topology and operational patterns. Per-path probability entries expose which next-hop nodes are reachable; the source PCE identifier (field 3) identifies the entity that computed the probability. Deployments in adversarial environments SHOULD consider omitting the source PCE identifier when source attribution is not required.

section.name: IANA Considerations
section.t: This document requests IANA to assign a new codepoint from the "Bundle Block Types" registry as defined in , Section 9.1, under the Specification Required registration policy ().

Suggested Value: The RFC authors suggest code point 0x1A (26 decimal) as a suitable unassigned value. The final value will be assigned by IANA upon publication; the value 0xC8 used throughout examples in this document is a non-normative placeholder. Implementations MUST NOT hardcode 0xC8 and SHOULD parameterize the block-type code so that the IANA-assigned value can be substituted post-publication.

This document additionally requests IANA to create a "CPB Metric Types" sub-registry with initial entries: 0=PRoPHET Delivery Predictability, 1=CGR Contact Confidence, 2=MaxProp Path Cost (inverted), 3=RAPID Utility Metric, 4=Generic Probability; values 5-255 unassigned.

section.name: Overhead Analysis

table.name: CPB Byte Overhead vs Payload Size

section.t: For kilobyte-scale payloads typical of DTN sensor data, overhead is below 3% even with full CPB fields.

section.name: Computational and Storage Overhead
section.t: The table above quantifies only wire-byte overhead. CPB consumption imposes additional costs on forwarders that SHOULD be considered when sizing a CPB-enabled deployment, particularly on constrained nodes:

dl.dd: Decoding the CPB map (up to 8 path entries) requires CBOR parsing of approximately 32-100 bytes per CPB. On commodity hardware this is sub-millisecond; on constrained microcontrollers with software floating-point it may be several milliseconds per CPB.

If the CPB is BPSec-protected, each consumption requires a signature verification. Public key verification (ECDSA, Ed25519, HMAC) costs vary by algorithm and hardware support. In the worst case (resource-constrained node, no hardware crypto), BIB verification can dominate CPB processing time. Implementations SHOULD cache verification results per (block-number, BIB-block-number) tuple within a single bundle's processing window.

Each new CPB observation potentially triggers route recomputation. For a confidence-weighted routing policy consuming CPB data (see CGR-UCoP as prior art), the cost is dominated by the contact-graph traversal, which scales as O(C log C) where C is the contact-plan size; CPB consumption adds a per-edge multiplication. The hysteresis and rate-limiting techniques of bound the recomputation rate.

If the strip-and-replace model () is not used, bundles can accumulate multiple CPBs across hops. Each CPB occupies up to ~32 bytes plus BIB overhead. Bundle store memory pressure SHOULD be considered when designing CPB production policy; the optional optimization in (a node appending a new CPB MAY remove earlier CPB instances) is relevant here.

Maintaining timestamp-aware probability decay () requires periodic re-evaluation of cached CPB values against the current clock. This is O(1) per cached CPB but the cache itself SHOULD have a bounded size.

section.t: On constrained DTN nodes, CPU and storage costs frequently exceed wire-byte costs in their operational impact. Concrete profiling numbers depend on the BP implementation, the cryptographic algorithms in use, and the deployment topology, and are not provided in this document. Implementations SHOULD publish their measured overhead alongside interoperability reports per .

section.t: This section records the status of implementations of the Contact Probability Block at the time of writing, in accordance with .

ul.li: Organization: Independent (N. Perry)
License: MIT License
Modules: cpb.py (encoder/decoder, ~600 LOC), test_cpb.py (23-test conformance suite), config1_sim.py (discrete-event simulator producing the results).

Coverage: Block structure (), block processing flags (), CBOR encoding rules (), invalid-float handling (), hex encoding table (), multiple-CPB precedence (), per-path matching (), CPB creation (), intermediate processing (), 8-entry DoS limit (), backwards compatibility ().

Maturity: Reference implementation. All 23 conformance tests pass on Python 3.10+ with cbor2 5.9.0. Byte-exact encoding match against and and the hex table in . Round-trip byte stability verified across multiple cycles.
Contact: nick@perrybrandsllc.com

dl.dd: Validation of CPB's routing impact was conducted via the pure-Python discrete-event simulator config1_sim.py, which implements both vanilla CGR (earliest-arrival) and several experimental consumers of CPB confidence data over a multi-asset adversarial Mars topology. reports the authoritative 80-seed adversarial massive topology study (12 rovers, 8 orbiters, 2 relays, 6 grounds). The simulator is fully deterministic per seed and reproduces to the digit on any Python 3.10+ environment with cbor2 installed. CGR-UCoP was used only as prior art for simulation parameters and basic validation.

dd.t: The author also installed and partially configured two production DTN reference implementations during the development of this specification. Neither produced data reported in this document; both are noted here for transparency:

ul.li: The ONE Simulator v1.6.0: Installed and a probability-aware Spray-and-Wait router (ProbabilityAwareSprayAndWaitRouter.java, ~250 LOC) was drafted. Across multiple Random Waypoint parameter sweeps the baseline and CPB-aware arms produced byte-identical outcomes, because the Spray-and-Wait spray decision differs from the baseline only when multi-neighbor encounters occur simultaneously - an event rare in sparse RWP topologies at the node counts tested. No results from The ONE are reported in . documents this configuration as deferred to follow-up work with denser topologies.

NASA ION (Interplanetary Overlay Network) v4.1.0: Installed and a minimal CPB-encoder integration was prototyped. End-to-end testing through ION's BP agent was not completed before this document was finalized; no results from ION integration are reported. Standard ION CGR behavior with respect to unknown extension blocks (discard if can't process flag) is consistent with the design in .

section.t: No other implementations are known to the author at the time of writing. Reports of new implementations are encouraged.

section.name: Experiment Description
section.t: This section describes the experiment by which the Contact Probability Block specification is validated. Per Section 4.2.1, an Experimental specification is accompanied by a description of the experiment in concrete, falsifiable terms.

section.name: Scope and Hypothesis
section.t: The experiment tests a single core hypothesis: that carrying per-contact probability metadata inside BPv7 bundles as an extension block enables routing protocols to deliver bundles that would otherwise be lost, in networks where contact opportunities are stochastic and multiple competing routes exist.
The primary metric is delivery ratio. End-to-end latency is reported as a secondary metric.

section.name: Test Configuration: Multi-Asset Mars Relay (CGR)
section.t: The experiment uses a multi-asset Mars-to-Earth relay topology with four surface assets, four orbiters, one deep-space relay, and three ground stations. All node identifiers in the topology use the "ipn" URI scheme as updated by ; node numbers shown are Default Allocator FQNNs.

section.name: Routing Policies Tested
section.t: CPB is a BPv7 extension block that carries per-contact probability metadata. The policies below are simulator-internal consumers of that metadata. CGR-UCoP is referenced only as prior art consulted during construction of the simulation parameters and for basic cross-validation; it is not the conceptual basis for the CPB block itself.

dl.dd: Standard Contact Graph Routing. The cost of a candidate route is its earliest predicted arrival time. Confidence values are ignored.
Experimental consumer of CPB data (metric-type 1) that also incorporates negotiated data rates. Route cost is computed as latency / (confidence × bottleneck_rate).
Stronger experimental consumer that adds an explicit quadratic penalty on low-confidence links: cost = latency + (1 − confidence)² × 5000.

PROPHET, MaxProp, and Spray-and-Wait style consumers. The PROPHET and MaxProp versions maintain protocol state (delivery predictability and path costs, respectively) and consult CPB confidence when available. The Spray-and-Wait version is more approximate due to simulator architecture constraints and is presented as directional evidence only (see ).

section.name: Methodology
section.t: The simulator is a Python implementation using the adversarial "massive" contact topology (12 rovers, 8 orbiters, 2 relays, 6 grounds) with contact success probabilities in the 0.55–0.72 range on the critical rover-orbiter hop and data rates generated independently of confidence. Each simulation runs for 7 days of simulated time with bundles generated every 30 s per rover after warm-up.
The study used 80 independent seeds on high-core x86 hardware. For each seed and each policy, the simulator executes over identical contact-failure realizations. The primary policies exercised were:

ul.li: Baseline (vanilla CGR): earliest-arrival routing with no use of per-contact confidence.
Rate-aware CPB consumer ("cpb"): cost = latency / rate + light explicit penalty on low confidence.
Risk-averse CPB consumer ("cpb-risk"): cost = latency + (1 − confidence)² × constant.

PROPHET-style, MaxProp-style, and Spray-and-Wait-style consumers, each implemented in two forms: a "classic" version that does not consult CPB confidence values, and a "cpb" version that additionally uses the confidence metadata carried in CPB blocks (metric-type 1) to initialize or adjust internal state (delivery predictability for PROPHET, path costs for MaxProp, spray-target selection for Spray-and-Wait).

section.name: Results
section.t: The study used the adversarial "massive" topology (12 rovers, 8 orbiters, 2 relays, 6 grounds) with contact success probabilities deliberately generated in the 0.55–0.72 range on the critical rover-orbiter hop and per-contact data rates generated independently of confidence. 80 independent seeds were executed on high-core x86 hardware.
For each seed, the following policies were exercised over identical contact-failure realizations:

ul.li: Baseline (vanilla CGR): confidence-blind earliest-arrival routing.
Rate-aware CPB consumer ("cpb").
Risk-averse CPB consumer ("cpb-risk").

PROPHET-style, MaxProp-style, and Spray-and-Wait-style consumers, each implemented in both a "classic" form (no use of CPB confidence) and a "cpb" form that additionally consults the per-contact confidence values carried in CPB blocks.

t.strong: Primary findings (80 seeds, adversarial massive topology):

ul.li: Baseline (vanilla CGR) delivery was 0.9762 with high tail latency (p95 ≈ 455 s).
The rate-aware CPB consumer ("cpb") and risk-averse CPB consumer ("cpb-risk") both achieved 0.9996 delivery with tight tails (p95 = 120 s).
PROPHET classic (no CPB): 0.9819 delivery, low average latency but poor tails (p95 ≈ 369 s). With CPB: 0.9996 delivery, p95 = 120 s.
MaxProp classic (no CPB): 0.9822 delivery, similarly optimistic latency but weak tails. With CPB: 0.9996 delivery, p95 = 120 s.

Spray-and-Wait classic (no CPB): 0.9663 delivery (worse than baseline) with anomalous latency behavior in early implementations. With CPB: 0.9946 delivery and materially improved tails (p95 ≈ 203 s). Even with the guard, Spray-and-Wait remains the weakest of the advanced consumers.

section.t: Interpretation. The data demonstrate that CPB confidence metadata provides substantial, consistent reliability gains to probabilistic routing protocols (PROPHET, MaxProp, and Spray-and-Wait) when they can consult it. In the absence of CPB, these protocols are optimistic: they achieve better latency on the bundles that succeed, but suffer materially higher loss rates and worse tails under adversarial conditions. When CPB confidence is available, they become better calibrated and the loss rate drops dramatically.

Limitations and caveats. The Spray-and-Wait implementations are the most constrained by the simulator architecture (bundle-centric rather than full per-node event-driven). Early versions produced anomalous (including negative) latency values; a runtime guard was added to enforce forward-looking route selection. The Spray-and-Wait results should therefore be treated as directional only. In operational deployments, Spray-and-Wait with CPB is best regarded as a method of last resort when more capable probability-aware forwarding is unavailable. The study also does not address noisy or adversarially supplied confidence values; those questions are left for future work.

ol.li: Determine whether CPB-enhanced routing improves delivery ratio under adversarial conditions with rate-aware costing. Met. In the 80-seed adversarial massive study, baseline delivery was 0.9762 while the CPB-augmented policies (cpb, cpb-risk, and the CPB-augmented versions of PROPHET and MaxProp) reached 0.9996, with the Spray-and-Wait CPB version reaching 0.9946. Gains were consistent across all 80 seeds.
Quantify CPB byte overhead. Met by analytical bounds: <3% for 1 KB+ payloads with full CPB.
Validate interoperability via byte-exact encoder. Met: 23 round-trip tests pass.
Assess float16 precision sufficiency. Met: binary16 quantization produces identical route selections under the tested policies in the configurations used.

Statistically significant improvement (p < 0.05). Met. The reliability gains for CPB-augmented policies versus baseline and versus the corresponding classic (no-CPB) versions of PROPHET, MaxProp, and Spray-and-Wait were consistent and large across all 80 seeds.
Sample size sufficient for the claims made. Met: 80 independent seeds on the adversarial massive topology, with each policy exercised over identical contact realizations per seed.
CPB byte overhead below 5% for 1 KB+ payloads. Met analytically.

No fundamental architectural conflicts with BPv7. Met technically: CPB is a standard extension block, EID immutability is preserved, BPSec integration is straightforward. Operational conflicts (trust framework, multi-domain CPB interaction, control-theoretic stability) are addressed at specification level but not closed by experimental demonstration.
No measurable improvement. Not triggered.
CPB byte overhead exceeds 10% for 1 KB payloads. Not triggered.
CBOR encoding incompatibilities. Not triggered.
BPSec integration produces irrecoverable failures. Not exercised in this configuration (deferred to follow-up work).

section.name: Deferred Configurations
section.t: Spray-and-Wait in mobile ad-hoc topology requires multi-neighbor concurrent encounters to differentiate from baseline; this regime is not produced by sparse Random Waypoint topologies at the node counts tested. Multi-CPB accumulation across 20 hops is a correctness test verified via byte-stable round-trips in the reference encoder; full end-to-end demonstration is deferred to integration work with a BPSec-enabled ION testbed.

section.name: Open Experimental Questions
section.t: The experiment in this document establishes baseline plausibility: confidence-weighted routing fed by accurate CPB data outperforms confidence-blind routing on the same contact-failure realizations. A complete validation of CPB as an operational standardized mechanism requires answering a series of follow-on questions that this document does not close. These are enumerated here so that reviewers, implementers, and follow-on researchers share a common list of what remains to be demonstrated.

dl.dd: The simulator uses ground-truth per-contact probabilities. Real deployments must estimate probabilities from historical observations or model predictions, both of which are noisy. Sensitivity analysis under varying estimator noise (e.g., additive Gaussian noise on confidences, biased estimators, estimator drift over time) is needed to characterize the operational regime where CPB-driven routing remains beneficial.

The age-threshold mechanism () defines when a CPB is discarded, but routing behavior just before the threshold fires (when probabilities are old but not yet invalid) is unstudied. A controlled experiment varying CPB staleness against routing outcome would inform the default max_age values.

The trust model () provides structural defenses, but their empirical effectiveness against specific attack patterns (sinkhole inflation, blackhole deflation, oscillation-induction, herding-induction) has not been measured. A red-team experiment with one or more adversarial CPB producers in the network would quantify the cost of attack vs. the cost of defense.
dl.dt: Conflicting CPBs from multiple administrative domains
dl.dd: defines policy options but does not demonstrate which option works in practice. A multi-domain testbed with explicit trust boundaries would characterize the gateway-translation, accept-all, and discard-all strategies under realistic traffic.

CPB is designed for incremental deployment: nodes that don't understand CPB pass it through unchanged. But the routing quality in a mixed CPB-aware / CPB-unaware network is not characterized. Sensitivity to the fraction of CPB-aware nodes would inform deployment phasing.

Probability-aware routing concentrates traffic on high-confidence routes (). Under sustained load this risks congestion collapse on the preferred routes and storage pressure at intermediate nodes. The mitigations of are RECOMMENDED but unmeasured. A high-load experiment varying bundle generation rate against delivery ratio would test the failure mode directly.

CPB has been designed not to interfere with BP custody transfer mechanisms (), but the combined behavior of custody-bound bundles carrying CPB data has not been exercised end-to-end. Particular attention should be paid to whether custody acknowledgments themselves carry CPB-relevant information and whether custody transfer policies should consume CPB.

defines CPB behavior under fragmentation, but only the reference Python encoder has been exercised against it. Real BP implementations (ION, HDTN, uPCN) have subtly different fragmentation pathways and CPB replication behavior across implementations is unproven.

This is the single largest standards-process gap. RFC publication at Experimental status is acceptable with simulator-only validation, but progression to Standards Track will require demonstrated interoperability between at least two independent implementations operating over real BPv7 stacks (canonically: NASA ION and an independently-developed alternative such as HDTN, µPCN, or a fresh implementation against this specification). The reference Python implementation () does not count as an independent implementation for this purpose, since it was developed alongside the specification by the same author.

identifies feedback dynamics qualitatively and recommends mitigations, but does not provide a formal stability proof. A control-theoretic analysis (e.g., describing the routing system as a discrete-time dynamical system with CPB-driven feedback and analyzing stability of fixed points) would substantially strengthen the standards case for CPB-driven routing in dense networks.

prohibits cross-metric arithmetic but does not validate the prohibition empirically. Whether a router making routing decisions from mixed-metric CPBs in practice produces worse outcomes than a router strictly partitioning by metric-type is an open empirical question.

section.t: Resolution of these questions is not a prerequisite for Experimental-track publication, but each will need to be addressed before the CPB mechanism can be reasonably considered for Standards Track. The author encourages the DTN research community to take up any subset of these as follow-on work; the reference implementation and simulator () provide a starting point for such studies.

section.name: Relationship to Updates of BPv7
section.t: (BPv7) has been updated by (administrative record types registry, January 2025) and (ipn URI scheme updates, May 2025) since this CPB work began. Neither update affects the wire format defined in :

ul.li: updates the "ipn" URI scheme. CPB implementations MUST encode and decode ipn EIDs per RFC 9758, including Default Allocator FQNNs. The LocalNode ipn URI form (Allocator=0, NodeNumber=2^32 - 1) has no meaning off-node and MUST NOT appear in CPB path-entries transmitted to other nodes.
RFC 9171 erratum 8376 notes that BPv7 ADU fragmentation interacts ambiguously with extension blocks. CPB's fragmentation handling is defined in .

section.name: Mars Mission Scenario
section.t: Consider a Mars rover (node 200) communicating with an Earth relay station via an orbiter (node 100):

ol.li: Initial contact: Rover creates a critical status bundle with a CPB indicating default probability 0.6 (dusty conditions), metric-type 1 (cgr-confidence), validity_duration 3600s
Rover-to-orbiter: Router at rover checks 0.6 < 0.7 -> wait for better conditions
Later contact: Dust clears, CPB is refreshed with probability 0.95, new timestamp
Orbiter processes: Router at orbiter checks 0.95 > 0.7 -> forward immediately
Result: Both bundles are delivered with minimal latency.

section.t: Decay example: If the first bundle (P=0.6) is delayed 10 hours and the validity_duration was 3600s, receiving routers recognize the CPB as expired and apply decay: P_aged = 0.6 * 0.98^10 = 0.49.
